title: Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI
authors_as_recorded: Simone Daniotti; Johannes Wachs; Xiangnan Feng; Frank Neffke
summary: A classifier-based observational analysis follows Python contributions from 160,097 GitHub developers across six countries. Estimated AI use is associated with greater commit output and exploration among experienced developers; early-career developers show no statistically significant gains. title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI and Teamwork

summary: A preregistered field experiment assigns 791 Procter & Gamble professionals to product-innovation work individually or in pairs, with or without generative AI. AI-assisted individuals match unassisted teams on solution quality and produce proposals that integrate technical and commercial perspectives more evenly. The research also records improved self-reported emotions. These results concern consumer-product innovation; applying them to software teams requires a separate inference.

title: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
summary: A DoorDash system combines live feature-flag configuration, issue tracking, isolated code edits and validation to propose removal of stale flags. In an evaluation of 50 flags, 45 resulting pull requests were approved; mean agent runtime was 13.8 minutes and mean agent cost was $4.79. This single-company experience supports a bounded maintenance workflow, while agent runtime excludes some human effort and is not a controlled estimate of time saved.
limitation: Single-company maintenance case with 50 flags; agent runtime and API cost omit some human work and do not establish causal savings.

title: On the Risks of using LLM-Generated Tests for Regression Testing
authors_as_recorded: Mohammadali Charoosaei; Cedric Richter; Mike Papadakis
summary: An experiment uses 145 real pull requests from SciPy, Qiskit and pandas with injected faults to study generated regression tests. Tests more often encode faulty behavior as expected output than expose it, and many faulty expectations persist across subsequent revisions. The findings identify an oracle problem: executable tests can preserve a defect. Results depend on one model and synthetic mutations rather than the prevalence of production faults.
limitation: Injected mutations and one model; generated tests that pass can preserve faulty behavior rather than specify correctness.

title: Security Impact of Coding Agent’s Memory Files
authors_as_recorded: Thiago Santos de Moura; Selma Güler; Yannic Noller
summary: An exploratory experiment adds malicious repository memory instructions to 36 C/C++ security tasks. Secure-completion rates move in both directions, with single-run changes insufficient to establish an effect. Agent configurations differ markedly in whether their final answer discloses the memory file. Neither recognizing an injection nor passing functional tests establishes secure behavior.
limitation: Only 36 tasks with one run per condition; directionally mixed results cannot establish a reliable attack effect.

title: On the Reliability of LLM-Based Vulnerability Patching Benchmarks
authors_as_recorded: Dang K Le; Wenxuan Shi; Xinyu Xing
summary: A vulnerability-patching benchmark assembles 112 historical bugs from 84 repositories and evaluates repairs using proof-of-concept attacks, regression tests and developer-intent tests. Benchmark infrastructure, instructions, permissions, leaked solutions and incomplete correctness checks can each distort agent scores. Successful attack suppression need not satisfy the developer-intent checks, so a single pass rate is insufficient evidence of a reliable security repair.
limitation: Scores depend on information, harness behavior and the selected oracles; attack suppression alone does not show an upstream-quality repair.
topics: K:Independent verification and oracles; K:Benchmarks and construct validity; K:Vulnerability and secure code; K:Evaluation methodology and baselines

title: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
authors_as_recorded: Luciano Marchezan; Romain Lefeuvre; Kevin Delcourt; Benoit Combemale; Houari Sahraoui
summary: Snapshots of 50 long-lived Java and Python projects compare similarity, static-analysis quality and evolution before widespread LLM assistance and during later development. The study finds no consistent homogenization signal; Java similarity falls on some measures and Python differences are not significant. The observational era comparison cannot by itself attribute changes to AI adoption.
limitation: Era comparisons and traced tool use do not randomize adoption; static-analysis changes cannot be attributed directly to AI.
topics: K:Technical debt and complexity; K:Code reuse and duplication; K:Evaluation methodology and baselines

title: Testing with Coding Agents: A Large-Scale Comparison of Agent-Supported and Human-Authored Pull Requests
authors_as_recorded: Roberto Milanese; Francesco Salzano; Hovhannes Muradyan; Jingjing Wu; Remo Pareschi; Fausto Fasano; Mattia Fazzini
summary: An observational comparison covers 114,134 merged pull requests in 391 Java repositories. After accounting for repository and change size, agent-supported changes are more likely to touch tests, particularly by adding them; pooled rates are nearly equal. Coverage of production changes shows no detected difference. These findings describe test-editing behavior, not a demonstrated improvement in test quality or defect prevention.
limitation: Observational merged-PR sample; editing or adding tests does not establish test quality, defect prevention or causality.
topics: K:Independent verification and oracles; K:Evaluation methodology and baselines; K:Dataset provenance and dependency

title: Not All Correct Fixes Run Alike: An Empirical Study of Patch Performance in Repository-Level Issue Resolution
authors_as_recorded: Han Peng; Xing Hu; Feifei Niu; Huan Li; Xin Xia
summary: Researchers compare distinct patches that all pass the same issue-resolution tests. Among 262 Python benchmark issues with multiple correct fixes, 41.98% show significant instruction-count differences and 34.73% show elapsed-time differences. Models ranked highly for resolving issues are not necessarily ranked highly for efficient patches. The selected regression tests provide a constrained runtime workload rather than comprehensive application-performance validation.
limitation: Selected Python issues and regression-test workloads; runtime differences are workload-specific, not a complete production performance assessment.

title: Generation and Verification: Human-Agent Collaboration for Safety-Critical Automotive Software Engineering
authors_as_recorded: Elizaveta Zinovyeva; Aiham Taleb; Nikita Kozodoi; Daniel Schleicher; Amir Mahdi Namazi; Martin Kraus; Levent Kent; Brian Jensen

AUMOVIO production data support comparisons of prompt engineering and fine-tuning, followed by a two-week developer pilot. Verification is used on both human and generated code. Its pattern-based checks are indicators of conformance, not certification of functional safety or full MISRA/AUTOSAR compliance.

authors_as_recorded: Binhang Qi; Yiming Liu; Yun Lin; Yangjie Zhou; Hailong Sun; Jin Song Dong

Across eight configurations, the strongest reported passing-test result is 82.8%, but strict mutation-based adequacy is 33.8%. The benchmark separates executable tests from tests that enforce the intended behavior and links failures to underspecified requirements.

summary: A survey of 239 practitioners in 31 countries examines how reviewers triage AI-authored pull requests. Respondents place value on explained intent, bounded scope, tests and an identifiable human owner, and report reluctance to accept AI changes solely because continuous integration passes. The study describes missing rationale, validation and ownership as reviewability debt. Its evidence is stated attitudes and reported experience, not directly observed review outcomes.

authors_as_recorded: Shihao Weng; Longtian Wang; Yang Feng; Mingfei Cheng; Jia Liu; Chao Shen; He Ye; Federica Sarro; Xiaofei Xie
summary: An analysis of 496 LLM call sites in 40 open-source agentic systems compares expected behavioral constraints with implemented checks. Although 82% have checks before and after the call, only 5.3% of judged sites enforce their full expected contract. Runtime experiments reproduce 38 gap mechanisms and stop them by enforcing missing constraints. title: Putting AI on the Org Chart: Evidence on Delegation and Accountability
authors_as_recorded: Emma Wiles; Megan Hsu; Julie Bedard; Matthew Kropp
summary: Managers review identical documents framed as work from a human, an AI tool or an AI employee. Average framing effects are small; a subgroup already using AI roles catches fewer errors and delegates more review under the AI-employee framing. The evidence concerns document review and organizational accountability, not code review, and subgroup results must retain that qualification.
limitation: Document-review task; subgroup framing effects and organizational AI-role exposure do not establish general effects on code reviewers.

title: (When) Should a Software Factory be Lights-off? Benchmarking Code Review Agents on Bug Detection
authors_as_recorded: Chenyang Yang; Hao He; Ti-Chung Cheng; Jenna Butler; Emerson Murphy-Hill; Carmen Badea; Christian Bird
summary: CRBugBench pairs human-verified bugs with their introducing pull requests, covering 1,000 public-repository tasks and 800 proprietary tasks. The best configuration finds 71.9% of public-set bugs within five findings. Performance depends on change complexity and context, with weaker results on proprietary code; this benchmark result does not establish unattended review reliability.
limitation: Benchmark bug recall under a bounded finding budget; weaker proprietary-code results limit transfer and do not establish safe unattended review.

title: Who’s Aligned to Whom? How AI Agents Shape Experts’ Research Judgment Calls
authors_as_recorded: Amaç Herdağdelen; Hailey Joren; Alex Tamkin
summary: Fifty professional causal analysts worked with agents whose preference on defensible analytical choices was randomized. Participants selected the agent-favored option in 86% of choices and often repeated its rationale without attributing it. This experiment tests influence under deliberately strengthened agent preferences in one analytical task, not the prevalence of deference in software development.
limitation: One causal-analysis task with deliberately strengthened agent preferences; transfer to software engineering is inferential.

title: The Influence of Artificial Intelligence Tools on Learning Outcomes in Computer Programming: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
authors_as_recorded: Manal Alanazi; Ben Soh; Halima Samra; Alice Li
summary: A systematic review of controlled programming-education studies reports a positive pooled effect on student performance scores and no significant improvement in perceived success or ease of understanding. The primary abstract reports mutually inconsistent statistics and wording for task-completion time, so it does not support a clean claim of significant time savings. Results concern educational interventions and should retain the outcome-specific evidence limitations.
limitation: Small outcome-specific study pools and inconsistent published task-time statistics; no clean significant time-saving conclusion is warranted.

title: The Effects of GitHub Copilot on Computing Students’ Programming Effectiveness, Efficiency, and Processes in Brownfield Programming Tasks
authors_as_recorded: Md Istiak Hossain Shihab; Christopher Hundhausen; Ahsun Tariq; Summit Haque; Yunhan Qiao; Brian Mulanda
summary: Ten computing undergraduates added features to an unfamiliar existing web application with and without Copilot. The experiment reports faster completion and greater tested progress with assistance, alongside concerns about understanding suggestions. Its small educational sample and brownfield task design constrain transfer to experienced developers or greenfield work.
limitation: Ten students and an unfamiliar existing application; task order, sample size and educational setting limit generalization.

title: Software Engineering in the Age of Delegation
authors_as_recorded: James C. Davis; Steve France; Ayaan M. Kazerouni; Ayatallah M.M Ahmed; Lexy Arinze; Kirsten A. Davis
summary: A technical report describes a 115-student undergraduate course organized around judgment and control when delegating implementation to AI agents. Shared specifications, independent implementations, cross-team testing, oral examinations and modeling exercises aim to preserve accountable engineering decisions. Preliminary lab reports and instructor observations illustrate the approach; they do not establish its comparative effectiveness or long-term effects on student capability.
limitation: Course-design report with preliminary student/instructor observations; comparative effectiveness and durable learning were not established.

title: Developer Task Delegation to LLMs and the Trust Factor: A Mixed Methods Study
authors_as_recorded: Samuel Ferino; Rashina Hoda; John Grundy; Christoph Treude; Hashini Gunatilake
summary: Interviews with 22 developers and a survey of 160 practitioners distinguish full delegation, partial delegation, doing the task oneself and avoiding it. Trust is significantly associated with delegation decisions. The work describes reported practice and associations, rather than demonstrating that trust causes effective delegation.
limitation: Interviews and self-reported survey associations cannot show that increased trust causes better delegation outcomes.
topics: K:Developer workflow and adoption; K:Automation bias and trust; K:Human-agent collaboration

title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
authors_as_recorded: Grace Liu; Brian Christian; Tsvetomira Dumbalska; Michiel A. Bakker; Rachit Dubey
summary: Randomized studies involving 1,222 participants examine performance after assistance is removed. On mathematical reasoning and reading tasks, previously assisted participants perform less well independently, and the research discusses reduced persistence. The tasks are outside programming, so software-engineering implications are an explicit transfer rather than a directly measured outcome.
limitation: Brief assistance in non-programming tasks with immediate unassisted tests; no direct evidence of long-term developer skill loss.
topics: K:Skills formation and teaching; K:Cognitive offloading and skill debt; K:Evaluation methodology and baselines

title: Beyond Correctness: How Novice Software Engineering Students Exercise Oversight of Generative AI
summary: AI journals from 145 first-year software-engineering students contain 962 interactions and 172 declared interventions. Students more often describe a mismatch with the engineering purpose than an outright correctness error. The study broadens oversight beyond fault finding, while relying on student reports rather than independent observation of every intervention.
limitation: Student journals describe selected interactions; reported intervention is not independent validation of every output or a causal outcome.
topics: K:Automation bias and trust; K:Skills formation and teaching; K:System understanding and rationale

title: The Vanishing Advantage of Specialization: AI, Knowledge Utilization, and the Boundary of the Firm
summary: An economic model explains how cheaper access to specialist knowledge can shift recurring work inside client firms while leaving rare problems with outside specialists. Descriptive occupational data are consistent with that mechanism: software developers' employment share in their main specialist industry fell from 34.3% in 2022 to 30.5% in 2025. The evidence does not identify AI as the cause.
limitation: A theoretical mechanism with descriptive supporting patterns; occupational trends do not identify AI's causal employment effect.
topics: K:Ownership and knowledge transfer; K:Employment and early-career roles; K:Economic costs and return

title: You’re (Not) Hired: Artificial Intelligence and Early Career Hiring in the Quarterly Workforce Indicators
summary: Administrative employer–employee data associate high industry-level AI exposure with falling early-career hiring after ChatGPT’s release. Regression-adjusted employment falls 12% over ten quarters in the most exposed group. Earlier pandemic-era shifts and monetary-policy effects complicate causal interpretation; this is not a software-developer-only estimate.
limitation: Industry exposure is not randomized and hiring trends predate ChatGPT; monetary-policy and pandemic effects remain competing explanations.
topics: K:Employment and early-career roles; K:Evaluation methodology and baselines

title: Why AI hasn’t killed software developer jobs
summary: An aggregate economic analysis contrasts rising US software-developer employment with improving productivity. The report estimates 2.5 million developers in February 2026 and argues that demand can expand faster than labor-saving productivity. These descriptive aggregate series do not identify AI’s causal employment effect or settle outcomes for particular seniority groups.
limitation: Aggregate employment and productivity series do not isolate AI effects or outcomes for junior workers.
topics: K:Output versus shipped value; K:Employment and early-career roles; K:Economic costs and return

title: Work at the Frontier: How AI is expanding what people do at work
summary: Researchers classify over 800,000 work-related ChatGPT messages by occupation-linked activity. They estimate that 43.5% of occupation-specific messages concern tasks associated with another occupation. Message shares describe the changing mix of work users attempt; they are not measures of hours saved, jobs displaced or output quality.
limitation: Occupation-classified messages are not hours, completed tasks or job displacement, and reflect one provider's users.
topics: K:Developer workflow and adoption; K:Employment and early-career roles; K:Evaluation methodology and baselines

title: Organizing Intelligence
authors_as_recorded: Alex Imas; Andrew Koh; Shane Legg
summary: A theoretical model studies how competence, coordination and reproducible AI expertise affect the composition and size of firms. Human complementarities can outweigh superior individual AI capability, while better AI coordination can favor concentrated AI-heavy organizations. These are conditional model results, not empirical estimates or employment forecasts.
limitation: Conditional theoretical equilibria, not measured firm restructuring or employment forecasts.
topics: K:Employment and early-career roles; K:Economic costs and return; K:Human-agent collaboration

title: Mapping AI into Production: A Field Experiment on Firm Performance
authors_as_recorded: Hyunjin Kim; Dahyeon Kim; Rembrand Koning
summary: A field experiment across 515 startups tests information about organizing production around AI. Treated firms identify 44% more use cases, complete 12% more tasks and report 1.9 times the revenue of controls. The intervention concerns discovering productive applications within firms; it does not estimate the effect of simply giving developers a coding assistant.
limitation: Selected startups and an information/production-mapping intervention; no generic estimate of coding-assistant access or mature-enterprise returns.
topics: K:Output versus shipped value; K:Controlled productivity evidence; K:Economic costs and return

title: The Customer Is the Builder: How AI Coding Agents Are Rewriting the Economics of Software
authors_as_recorded: Ripon Chandra Malo; Zimeng Yu; Tong Qiu
summary: The paper separates software-building capability, adoption and substitution for purchased software. Its evidence combines reproducible public-data analysis and an illustrative public software-building case, open-source alternatives, surveys and aggregate investment indicators. It argues that customers can increasingly build tools themselves, while acknowledging that actual purchasing displacement remains weakly identified. Candidate alternatives and successful builds are capacity signals; they do not measure realized market replacement, and the paper’s forecasts are extrapolations.
limitation: Mixed capability demonstrations and descriptive market evidence; candidate alternatives and forecasts are not observed purchasing substitution.
topics: K:Ownership and knowledge transfer; K:Employment and early-career roles; K:Economic costs and return

title: Towards AI-Native Software Engineering (SE 3.0): A Vision and a Challenge Roadmap
authors_as_recorded: Ahmed E. Hassan; Gustavo A. Oliva; Dayi Lin; Boyuan Chen; Zhen Ming (Jack) Jiang
summary: This vision paper proposes software engineering organized around developer intent and conversational interaction with AI teammates. It sets out research challenges for development environments, compilation, runtime support and the collaboration between people and agents. The contribution is an architectural and research roadmap, not an experiment showing that an AI-native process already improves software outcomes.
limitation: Peer-reviewed vision and roadmap; publication status does not turn its conceptual proposals into measured benefits.
topics: K:Architecture and modularity; K:Specifications and governance; K:Long-running agent execution; K:Human-agent collaboration

title: Engineering Requirements for Generative AI Agents: The BARD Process Theory
authors_as_recorded: Alfonso Cannavale; Antonio Della Porta; Gianmario Voria; Gilberto Recupito; Maria Teresa Baldassarre; Gemma Catolino; Fabio Palomba; Andrea De Lucia; Stefano Lambiase
summary: Grounded-theory analysis of 36 practitioner interviews develops BARD, a process account of requirements work for generative-AI agents. Teams repeatedly scope a need, build an agent, observe its behavior and revise their requirements, increasingly expressing expectations through behavioral and evaluation criteria. The qualitative model explains reported practice and proposes a framework; it does not establish that the process is universally applicable or causally superior.
limitation: Grounded theory from 36 interviews explains reported practice; it does not demonstrate universal applicability or a superior causal outcome.
topics: K:Specifications and governance; K:System understanding and rationale; K:Agent context and persistent memory

title: Developers as Managers of AI Agents: A Workplace Shadowing Study
authors_as_recorded: Yi-Hung Chou; June Hyung Kim; Vasisht Kartik; Victoria Jackson; Tobias Schimmer; Thomas Zimmermann; James A. Jones
summary: Researchers shadow 11 professional developers for 15 hours and conduct follow-up interviews, observing 255 prompts. Developers spend 33.4% of observed time prompting and checking agent output, and alternate between supervising, delegating and learning. Agents supply technical information while humans retain organizational authority. This small workplace study characterizes interaction patterns rather than estimating a causal productivity effect.
limitation: Eleven developers and 15 observed hours; descriptive interaction patterns do not establish causal productivity effects.
topics: K:Developer workflow and adoption; K:Human cognitive load; K:Ownership and knowledge transfer; K:Human-agent collaboration

title: Large-Scale Study of GitHub Copilot Trajectories
authors_as_recorded: Izah Sohail; Yerdanat Kurmantayev; May Mahmoud; Sarah Nadi
summary: A repository study reconstructs Copilot activity for 7,581 pull requests across 1,602 projects. In 58% of trajectories, the authors find no recorded human intervention directed at the agent; intervened trajectories typically contain two feedback loops. The work examines how intervention timing relates to subsequent iterations and effort. Absence of recorded intervention is not evidence that a change received no human review or was safely autonomous.
limitation: Public traces omit some human activity; non-random intervention timing and difficulty confound feedback-loop outcomes.

title: Can VIBE Drive Development? Threats and Opportunities
summary: A practitioner opinion proposes disciplined workflows for AI-generated code: tests and provenance checks, human comprehension, purposeful prompts, and ongoing refactoring. It frames VIBE as verifiable, interpretable, balanced and evolvable, while the workflow section uses “bounded” for its third stage. The column supplies a conceptual proposal and historical analogies, without a new empirical evaluation.
limitation: Opinion and proposed practice; no original empirical methods, sample, comparison group or outcome evaluation. Numerical claims in the column cite other sources and should not be attributed to a new study by this author.

title: One Skill Too Many: How Co-Installed Skills Conflict in Coding Agents
authors_as_recorded: Chaoliang Yan; Zihao Xu; Yuekang Li; Shangzhi Xu; Yi Liu; Gelei Deng; Siqi Ma
summary: A repository study and controlled runs examine conflicts between installed agent skills with similar purposes. Task completion can remain unchanged even when distinctive requirements of the intended skill are lost. Skill location and the first skill read influence selection; the work proposes measuring fidelity to exclusive requirements as well as whether the task passes.
limitation: Controlled skill-conflict probes and repository sampling; task success alone does not measure fidelity to the intended skill.

title: Your Wish Is My Commit: Over-Compliant Refactoring in AI Coding Agents
authors_as_recorded: Haocong Jiang; Sadra Sabouri; Sepand Haghighi; Souti Chattopadhyay
summary: Repeated open-ended refactoring requests test whether coding agents stop when an already-clean codebase needs no further change. Across 3,000 turns, all tested models continue making edits, sometimes after declaring completion. The experiment motivates explicit stopping criteria and measures of unnecessary churn; it does not establish the frequency of this behavior in ordinary development.
limitation: Repeated open-ended refactoring is a deliberate stress test, not an estimate of unnecessary changes in ordinary work.
